chapter: Blood, Sweat & Tears and Horace Silver
title: What Horace Silver taught about writing and soloing
summary: Silver turned life into compositions, wrote lyrics, and coached soloists to play short; he stopped a take of 'Prescription for the Blues' for too many notes.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Did it help your compositional approach to play in that band?

I think it did because Horace had a way of turning his life experience, particularly his travel experience, into music. So you might get a tune called “Tokyo Blues” that has some kind of harmonic influence, or women that he had met along the way, or things that happened to him, “Song for my Father” you know written for his father. He had a way of interpreting his life’s experience into music. And he also was very influential to me in that as a hobby, well it wasn’t really a hobby because he started utilizing lyrics to his tunes so in his spare time on the buses or on the vans he was writing lyrics that he utilized. So I took that to heart too and started writing lyrics. He also was very — he knew what he wanted from a soloist on certain tunes. I mean he was very active in coaching us on certain tunes where he just wanted a funky solo, not many notes. On other tunes we could play what we wanted but on specific tunes he’d get mad if we played too long or we played too many notes. I remember there was a record we did with my brother called “Prescription for the Blues.”

And I don’t remember the name of the tune but he gave us the lecture before we started about, “I don’t want to hear too many notes, I don’t want to hear 16th notes. You know keep your solos short. And Mike was playing away on one tune, burning, with Louis Hayes on drums, Ron Carter on bass, and Horace stopped the take and made us start over. “Too many notes, I told you, I don’t want 16th notes.”

Yeah he was hands on in that department. Other guys, Art Blakey never said a word but he was very — he knew what he wanted from tune to tune. And there were tunes, like I said, that were specifically open, we could do whatever we wanted. And then he didn’t say anything.
